prompt: A consumer acks a message and then does the work. It crashes between the two. What happens to that message?
hint: Does Pub/Sub still have it?

choices.text: It is processed twice
choices.why: That is the other order: work first, then ack.

choices.text: It is lost: Pub/Sub forgot it at the ack
choices.why: Right: at most once. Nothing is done twice, and this message is never processed.

choices.text: Pub/Sub notices the crash and delivers it again
choices.why: After the ack Pub/Sub has nothing left to deliver; it knows nothing of the consumer's work.

choices.text: It is processed exactly once
choices.why: No ordering of the two steps gives that; here the work never happened.

prompt: Why is "exactly once" not a third way of ordering the work and the ack?
hint: The two writes go to different systems.

choices.text: Because the ack has to come first
choices.why: It can come in either order; that is what the two guarantees are.

choices.text: Because it needs a faster network
choices.why: Speed makes the window smaller and never closes it.

choices.text: No single write covers both
choices.why: Right: a crash between them either loses or repeats. Exactly once is built from atomic writes or idempotent work, end to end.

choices.text: Because Pub/Sub forbids it in its terms of use
choices.why: It is a matter of two separate writes, not of a rule.

prompt: Why is at least once the default for everything Quitanda counts?
hint: Which of the two failures can be repaired afterwards?

choices.text: It is cheaper to run than at most once
choices.why: Both cost the same to run; they differ in what a crash does.

choices.text: Pub/Sub removes the duplicates on its own
choices.why: It does not, and the lesson's replay showed the totals going wrong without a dedupe.

choices.text: It is the one that loses nothing
choices.why: Right: duplicates can be removed afterwards, lost messages cannot. At most once fits only data that may be lost.

choices.text: It keeps messages in order
choices.why: Order is a separate problem, solved by an ordering key.

prompt: A publisher sends `o-301` twice because the first answer was lost. Which key tells the two messages apart from two real payments?
hint: The two copies got different message ids.

choices.text: The message id Pub/Sub assigned
choices.why: The copy got a new id, 2 against 1, so to Pub/Sub they are two events.

choices.text: The publish time of each message
choices.why: Each copy has its own publish time, and two real payments a second apart would too.

choices.text: The order id in the data
choices.why: Right: an order is paid once, so a second message for the same order is a duplicate.

choices.text: The ack id of the delivery
choices.why: An ack id names one delivery to a subscriber, and is new on every delivery.

prompt: In the lesson, a second `gcloud pubsub subscriptions pull` right after the first took about ten seconds and returned the same two messages. Why?
hint: What had happened to them in the first pull?

choices.text: Their ten-second deadline ran out
choices.why: Right: the same message ids came back under new ack ids 3 and 4.

choices.text: The emulator was slow to answer the first time
choices.why: It was already running; the wait was the deadline, the same length as `ackDeadlineSeconds`.

choices.text: The publisher sent the two messages again
choices.why: Nothing was published between the pulls, and the ids were the same.

choices.text: The first pull had acked them already
choices.why: It printed ack ids without acking; an acked message is not delivered again.

prompt: A consumer of an ordered subscription needs 25 seconds per message and is written with unary pulls, on a 10-second deadline. What should it do?
hint: Unary pulls have nobody extending their leases.

choices.text: Ack before doing the work
choices.why: That stops the redelivery by making the consumer at most once, which loses a message on every crash.

choices.text: Nothing, since an ordered subscription waits for the consumer
choices.why: Order does not extend a deadline; an expired one redelivers the message and the key's later ones.

choices.text: Lower the retention of the subscription
choices.why: Retention decides how long a message is kept, not how long a consumer holds it.

choices.text: Extend the deadline while it works
choices.why: Right: that is what the streaming client does on its own; in the lesson, sixty seconds kept the messages away for twenty.

prompt: Which of these put the same payment into a consumer's hands twice? Choose all that apply.
hint: Five places were named, and two things that look like duplicates and are not.

choices.text: A publisher that retries after a lost answer
choices.why: Right; the topic holds both copies, with two ids.

choices.text: A consumer that dies before its ack
choices.why: Right; the messages come back once the deadline runs out.

choices.text: A push endpoint that answers 503
choices.why: Right; message 17 of lesson 19 arrived three times.

choices.text: Two customers paying the same amount on the same day
choices.why: Those are two real events, not a duplicate.

choices.text: Two events of one order delivered out of order
choices.why: That is an ordering problem; each event arrived once.

prompt: `totals.py plain 4` crashed, and the restart straight after it found no messages at all. Why?
hint: Who held the seven messages at that moment?

choices.text: The crash had acknowledged them
choices.why: The crash came before the ack; ten seconds later all seven were delivered again.

choices.text: They were still lent to the dead process
choices.why: Right: Pub/Sub cannot tell a dead consumer from a slow one, so it waits out the deadline.

choices.text: The snapshot had removed them from the subscription
choices.why: A snapshot removes nothing; it records a position to seek back to.

choices.text: SQLite locked the subscription
choices.why: The database knows nothing about Pub/Sub.

prompt: In `plain` mode, `o-301` (4,590), `o-303` (990, published twice) and `o-306` (7,200) are `c-17`'s payments. The first run added four messages before crashing, the second added all seven. What total did `c-17` end with, in cents?
hint: `o-301` was added twice, and each copy of `o-303` twice.

prompt: With the dedupe by message id, `c-17` came out at 13,770 instead of 12,780. What slipped through?
hint: Which duplicate kept its message id, and which got a new one?

choices.text: The redelivery after the crash
choices.why: That one was caught: ids 3 to 6 were refused on the second run.

choices.text: The publisher's second `o-303`
choices.why: Right: 13,770 is 12,780 plus a second 990.

choices.text: The payment of `c-05`
choices.why: `c-05` was right in every run; its total is 2,350.

choices.text: A message the snapshot did not hold
choices.why: The snapshot held all seven; the run read seven.

prompt: `totals.py` records the order id in `processed` and adds to the total inside one `with db:` transaction. What goes wrong if the two are committed separately, the key first?
hint: Put a crash between the two commits.

choices.text: The order is recorded and never counted
choices.why: Right: on the redelivery the key is already there, so the payment is skipped for good.

choices.text: Nothing, since the redelivery repairs it
choices.why: The redelivery meets the recorded key and skips the payment; nothing repairs it.

choices.text: SQLite refuses two commits for one message
choices.why: SQLite commits whatever it is asked; the gap is the consumer's design.

choices.text: The order is counted twice
choices.why: That is the gap in the other order, the total first and the key second.

prompt: `sink.py put c-09 500` was run twice. What does the row hold?
hint: An upsert sets, an increment adds.

choices.why: Right: the second write replaced 500 with 500.
That is `add` twice, the write that is not idempotent.

choices.text: An error, since the key exists
choices.why: `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` turns the clash into an update.

choices.text: Two rows of 500
choices.why: `customer_id` is the primary key, so there is one row.

prompt: Why does an upsert not suit Quitanda's payments stream as it is?
hint: What does each event carry: a state or a change?

choices.text: SQLite has no upsert
choices.why: It has one; `sink.py put` is it.

choices.text: Upserts are slower than inserts, and the stream is busy
choices.why: Speed is not the obstacle; the content of the event is.

choices.text: A payment is a change, not the new balance
choices.why: Right: to upsert, the publisher would have to send the balance itself, which it does not know.

choices.text: An upsert loses the order id
choices.why: The key of the row decides what is kept, and an order id fits in a row like anything else.

prompt: A consumer writes each pulled batch to Cloud Storage under the SHA-256 of the batch. Why does a redelivery from Pub/Sub still leave the same payment in two objects?
hint: Does a redelivery rebuild the same batch?

choices.text: The hash is different on every run
choices.why: SHA-256 of the same bytes is the same; the lesson's two copies landed on one name.

choices.text: A redelivery groups the messages differently
choices.why: Right: a subscription has no positions to batch by, so the content name changes with the grouping.

choices.text: fake-gcs-server never overwrites an existing object
choices.why: It did: the second copy replaced the first under one name.

choices.text: Cloud Storage refuses to overwrite objects
choices.why: An overwrite is silent and final, as lesson 1 warned; that is what made the content name work.

prompt: What did the exactly-once subscription do that the ordinary one did not?
hint: Both redelivered message 10.

choices.text: Refused the ack with the expired ack id
choices.why: Right, with `EXACTLY_ONCE_ACKID_FAILURE`; the ordinary one accepted it and said nothing.

choices.text: Did not redeliver after the deadline
choices.why: It redelivered just the same; the promise is about no redelivery before the deadline, and none after a successful ack.

choices.text: Removed the publisher's second copy
choices.why: Ids 11 and 12 were both delivered.

choices.text: Delivered in order
choices.why: Order is the ordering key's business, a different setting.

prompt: Which of these does exactly-once delivery cover?
hint: Read the promise in `gcloud`'s help: it is about one message id.

choices.text: A publisher's retry that stored a payment twice
choices.why: The copies have two ids, and both were delivered.

choices.text: A push endpoint that answered 503
choices.why: Push subscriptions do not offer exactly-once delivery.

choices.text: A consumer that adds a payment and dies before it acks
choices.why: The redelivery comes after the deadline, and the work is repeated; the effect is still the consumer's.

choices.text: A message acked with success, on a pull subscription in one region
choices.why: Right: that message is not delivered to the subscription again.

prompt: An order's status events sometimes arrive out of order, and a `delivered` must never be overwritten by a late `packed`. What does the sink need?
hint: The dedupe tests existence; this test compares.

choices.text: Exactly-once delivery on the subscription
choices.why: It prevents redelivery of one id and does nothing about the order of two different messages.

choices.text: A dedupe table keyed by order id
choices.why: That would refuse every event of the order after the first, `delivered` included.

choices.text: A version from the publisher, and a write applied only if newer
choices.why: Right: `UPDATE ... WHERE version < ?` keeps the newest status whatever order they arrive in.

choices.text: A longer ack deadline
choices.why: A deadline is about one delivery; it does not order two messages.

prompt: Match each source of duplicates to what catches it.
hint: One of them keeps its message id.

pairs.right: An idempotency key in the data
A dedupe on the message id

pairs.left: A replay with seek into an upsert
pairs.right: Nothing more: the sink is idempotent

pairs.left: A Cloud Storage subscription writing twice
pairs.right: A dedupe when the lake is compacted

prompt: Put in order what `totals.py by-order-id` does with one pulled batch.
hint: The ack is last, once per batch.
items: Pull up to ten messages from `totals`
Parse each message's order id, customer and amount
In one transaction, insert the order id and add the amount
If the insert breaks the primary key, report a duplicate and add nothing

prompt: A write is ___ when repeating it leaves the same result as doing it once.
hint: The word the lesson's title ends on, almost.

prompt: A colleague proposes switching on exactly-once delivery on `totals` and removing the `processed` table. Which run of the lesson shows the totals would then go wrong?
hint: Which duplicate does exactly-once delivery not see?

choices.text: The by-message-id run, where the publisher's second `o-303` was added
choices.why: Right: two ids for one payment, and exactly-once delivery delivered both copies in its own section too.

choices.text: The run of `sink.py put`
choices.why: That sink is idempotent; it has nothing to do with `totals`.

choices.text: None; exactly-once delivery covers every duplicate
choices.why: It covers the redelivery of one id, and the lesson showed two ids delivered.

choices.text: The push test of lesson 19
choices.why: Push does not offer exactly-once delivery at all, and `totals` is a pull subscription.
